title: Errors in a member community
metaTitle: Say what broke in a member community
excerpt: When a member hits an error while deciding to post, say what broke and what to do next. A code and a sad illustration waste the moment they were willing to speak.
alt: Five people working on laptops around a wooden table, a working group that still needs a plain sentence when a post fails.
caption: The work is on the table. The error should stay there too. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a community say when a post fails to send?
faqs.answer: Say that the post did not send, and say whether the draft is still in the composer. Offer one next step, usually try again. Leave the text, the room, and any attachment in place. A toast that says "Error" and then disappears trains people to screenshot the failure and give up on posting.

faqs.question: Should an error use an illustration?
faqs.answer: An illustration can sit beside the message. It cannot be the message. A sad face or a broken robot does not say whether the draft survived, whether the room rejected the post, or what to tap next. The words have to carry the screen for someone who does not see the picture.

faqs.question: How is an error different from a permission?
faqs.answer: An error means something the person was allowed to do did not succeed. A permission means they were never allowed to do it, and the interface should have said so before they wrote the post. If the real cause is a room rule, say the rule. Do not disguise a rule as a random failure.

markdown:
Member community error states are the sentences a person reads when a post, a reply, or an upload fails while they are still deciding whether to speak. Say what broke and what to do. A status code and a sad illustration waste the only moment they were willing to try.

The draft they typed has to still be there. The next action has to be smaller than the courage it took to write. If the screen clears the text and shrugs, they will go back to lurking. They will be right to. The product just taught them that speaking is risky in a way that has nothing to do with the room.

## Say what broke, in the room's language

Name the object that failed. The reply did not post. The photo did not attach. The intro did not send. "Something went wrong" is a refusal to look at the failure. The member cannot fix a something.

Say the cause in words they can act on. The connection dropped. The file is larger than this room allows. That thread was removed while they were writing. You do not need the server's name for the exception. You need the fact that changes their next tap.

Then say the next action in the same sentence or the one after it. Try again. Choose a smaller file. Write it in a thread that is still open. One action. A paragraph of apology with three equal buttons is another decision, and they are already tired.

Keep the nouns you used on the successful path. If the button said Reply, the error says the reply did not post. "Record insert failed" is the database talking through the interface. The member does not have a record. They have a reply they hoped someone would read.

The W3C describes the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines as a shared standard so content is perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. An error that lives only in a picture, or only in a color, fails that standard in spirit and often in the criteria. [The WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) is the document to keep open while you write these sentences. The message has to be text. It has to say what is wrong. It has to be understandable without a teammate translating a code.

## The draft has to survive the failure

The cruel version of this screen clears the composer and shows a toast. The toast leaves. The words are gone. The member now has two problems: the post failed, and the product destroyed the work. They will not rewrite it. They will lurk, or they will paste from a notes app they start keeping out of distrust.

Hold the draft in the composer. Hold the room they were posting to. Hold the attachment, or say clearly that the attachment has to be chosen again and why. If you can retry without asking them to tap, you may still tell them you are retrying. Silence plus a spinner is not a sentence.

If the failure is partial, say which part worked. The text posted and the image did not. The reply posted and the mention did not notify. "Some of this failed" is unfinished until you name the part. People will assume the worst part failed, which is usually the words they cared about.

Do not send them to the feed to "check" whether it worked. The feed is a scavenger hunt. The composer, or a posted object they can see, is the proof. One truth, visible in the message and in the thread.

## The failures worth writing before launch

You do not need a unique illustration for every failure. You need a sentence for each one that a member will actually hit in the first week.

The connection drops while they are composing. This will happen on a phone in a hallway. The copy should assume the draft is local until the post succeeds, and it should say so.

The file is too large, or it is a type the room does not accept. Name the limit in the unit they understand. "That video is too large to attach. Post the reply without it, or choose a shorter clip." A bare "415" is how engineers talk to each other.

The thread disappeared while they were replying. A moderator removed it, or the author did. Say that the thread is gone and offer the draft so they can post it somewhere else if they still want to. Deleting their words because the parent vanished is a second injury.

They tap Post twice because the first tap felt ignored. Say that the reply is already posted, and take them to it. A second copy, or a scolding, punishes a slow network.

A rate limit or a moderation hold is a special case. If a person can see their post and other members cannot yet, say that. "Your reply is waiting for a moderator" is a status. "Error" is a lie. If they are posting too fast for the room's rule, say the rule in human time. "You can post again in a minute" is a rule. A locked button with no reason is a bug wearing a rule's clothes.

Write these as a list in the design file, next to the happy path, with the real sentences:

- Reply failed, draft kept, try again
- Attachment rejected, text kept, what to change
- Thread gone, draft kept, where else to put it
- Duplicate tap, reply already there
- Held for review, what "held" means

If a failure cannot happen, say so on the list so nobody invents a cute empty state for it. If it can happen, the list is unfinished until the sentence is the one in the build.

## Where the message sits

Put the message at the point of failure. A problem with the link they pasted belongs on that field. A problem with the send belongs on the send button, without jumping them to the top of a long screen they have now scrolled away from.

On a phone, the message has to be in the same view as the action. A banner at the top of the page, behind the keyboard, does not exist for the person who is typing. Anchor it to the composer they are looking at.

Toasts are a poor home for this news. They leave on a timer, they are easy to miss, and they rarely have room for the draft's fate plus the next step. A toast can confirm a small success. It should not be the only record of a failed post.

Color can support the message. Red, or whatever your warning color is, cannot be the message. Someone who does not see that color still needs the sentence. An icon with no text fails the same way. Write the words first. Add the mark second.

Do not play a joke. A community error is a social moment. They were about to be seen, and then they were not. A pun about a lost carrier pigeon makes the product look as if it finds their embarrassment funny. Be plain. Plain is kinder.

## What a code and a mascot cost you

A code is useful in a log. It is rarely useful in the composer. If support needs a reference, put a short reference in small type under the sentence, after the human part. Do not lead with it. The member's first job is to recover the post, not to file a ticket.

A full-screen illustration replaces the room with a mood. The room was the product. Coming back from that screen should be obvious, and the draft should be waiting. If your error template is a centered picture, a one-word headline, and a button that says Go home, you have designed a dead end for the exact person who was about to participate.

"Go home" is often the wrong recovery. Home may be a feed that does not contain their draft. The recovery is Try again, or Back to the thread. Home is an escape hatch for people who are done, not the repair.

Read the copy out loud as if you had just written something personal and the send failed. If you would feel brushed off, the copy is wrong. If you would know what to do with your thumb, it is close enough to ship.

## Review the failures, then separate the rules

Build a fresh member on a phone. Throttle the network. Write a two-sentence reply. Cut the connection. Post. You are looking for three things: the draft is still there, the sentence names the failure, and one control retries or saves without making them retype.

Repeat for an oversized file and for a thread you delete while the reply is open. Those two catch the partial failure and the vanished parent. They take less time than a meeting about the tone of the mascot.

Some of what you will find are not errors. The member was not allowed to post in that room, and the product let them write anyway. That is a permission shown too late. The next piece is [permissions in a member community](/blog/permissions-in-a-member-community), because a hidden or unexplained rule feels exactly like a bug, and members will report it as one.

If these sentences are still unwritten and you want them treated as part of the interface, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). The failure copy is part of finishing the room. It is not a polish pass you schedule after the first real member has already been embarrassed.
